CourseName: CEN3722 - Introduction to Human Computer Interfaces

Outcomes.Text: Explain the purpose and core features of Figma as a UI/UX prototyping tool.
Apply frames and layout grids to structure high-fidelity interface screens.
Create reusable components and component variants to maintain design consistency.
Demonstrate auto-layout techniques to build responsive and adaptive interface elements.
Identify appropriate interactive prototype connections and transitions for user flow communication.
Evaluate a peer's Figma prototype against usability and design consistency criteria.

Topics.Title: Introduction to Figma and the Prototyping Workflow
Topics.Summary: Orients students to the Figma interface and establishes the end-to-end workflow from blank canvas to shareable prototype. Covers the key panels, tools, and file organisation conventions used throughout the module.

Elements.Title: The Figma Interface at a Glance
Elements.BodyText: Figma's browser-based environment is divided into a toolbar, layers panel, canvas, and properties panel, all of which work together in real time.
Elements.Notes: Point out that Figma runs entirely in the browser, eliminating version-control headaches common with desktop-only tools. Mention the Figma desktop app as an optional alternative.

Items.Text: The left panel shows layers, pages, and assets for the current file.
The canvas is infinite and supports multiple pages within one file.
The right properties panel changes contextually depending on what is selected.
The toolbar at the top provides quick access to frames, shapes, text, and component tools.

Elements.Title: Pages and File Organisation
Elements.BodyText: Organising work across named pages and clearly labelled frames keeps large projects navigable and supports smooth handoff to developers or evaluators.
Elements.Notes: A common convention is to dedicate one page to the design system, one to wireframes, and separate pages to each major user flow. Encourage teams to agree on naming conventions early.

Items.Text: Pages act as tabs within a single Figma file and can represent different stages or sections of a project.
Consistent frame naming makes it easier for collaborators to navigate and for prototypes to link correctly.
Grouping related frames with a cover frame or section label improves readability in presentation mode.

Elements.Title: Collaboration and Sharing Basics
Elements.BodyText: Figma is built around real-time multiplayer collaboration, allowing team members and evaluators to view, comment on, or edit a file simultaneously.
Elements.Notes: Share links can be set to view-only or edit access. For peer evaluation, view-only links protect the original design while still allowing comments.

Items.Text: Shareable links can be scoped to view, comment, or edit permissions.
Multiple cursors appear on canvas when collaborators are active, enabling live co-design sessions.
Comments can be pinned directly to canvas elements to provide contextual feedback.
Version history lets teams roll back to any previously saved state of the file.

Elements.Title: From Mockup to Prototype: The Module Workflow
Elements.BodyText: This module follows a structured sequence: framing screens, building a component library, applying auto-layout, and finally wiring interactions into a navigable prototype.
Elements.Notes: Emphasise that each stage builds on the previous one. Students who skip component setup often face time-consuming rework when making global design changes later.

Items.Text: Stage one focuses on frame setup and screen layout using grids.
Stage two establishes reusable components before detailed design begins.
Stage three applies auto-layout to make elements responsive to content changes.
Stage four connects screens with interactions to produce a testable prototype.

Topics.Title: Frames, Grids, and Screen Layout
Topics.Summary: Teaches students to use Figma frames as the foundational container for every screen, and to apply layout grids and constraints to ensure consistent, device-appropriate designs.

Elements.Title: What Is a Frame?
Elements.BodyText: In Figma, a frame is the primary artboard-like container that defines the boundaries of a screen, dialog, or component, and it carries layout and clipping properties not available to basic groups.
Elements.Notes: Frames can be nested inside other frames, which is the basis for component and auto-layout architecture. Distinguish frames from groups early to avoid student confusion.

Items.Text: Frames can be given fixed dimensions matching device presets such as iPhone, desktop, or tablet.
Frames clip their contents by default, preventing elements from spilling outside the defined screen boundary.
Nested frames are the building blocks for components and auto-layout containers.
Frames appear as distinct nodes in the prototype flow, whereas groups do not.

Elements.Title: Applying Layout Grids
Elements.BodyText: Layout grids overlay the frame canvas with columns, rows, or a uniform grid, giving designers a visual alignment scaffold that can be hidden before handoff or presentation.
Elements.Notes: A 12-column grid at 375 px width with 16 px gutters mirrors Bootstrap's mobile grid and provides a familiar reference. Grids are non-destructive and do not affect export.

Items.Text: Column grids define horizontal divisions used to align text, images, and interactive elements.
Gutter and margin settings control spacing between and around columns.
Multiple grids can be stacked on a single frame for complex layout requirements.
Grids are visible only in the editor and do not appear in exported assets or prototype previews by default.

Elements.Title: Constraints and Responsive Anchoring
Elements.BodyText: Constraints determine how child elements reposition or resize when their parent frame is resized, laying the groundwork for designs that adapt across screen sizes.
Elements.Notes: Constraints work on a per-element basis. Setting an element to 'Left and Right' makes it stretch horizontally when the frame widens — a simple form of responsiveness before auto-layout is introduced.

Items.Text: Horizontal constraints include Left, Right, Left and Right, Center, and Scale options.
Vertical constraints mirror horizontal options and control top, bottom, and stretch behaviour.
Combining constraints with fixed dimensions can pin elements like navigation bars to the top of a screen.
Constraints are superseded by auto-layout rules when both are applied to the same element.

Elements.Title: Working with Device Presets and Safe Areas
Elements.BodyText: Figma's frame presets provide accurate pixel dimensions for common devices, and designers must account for system UI areas such as status bars and home indicators.
Elements.Notes: The iOS safe area is 44 px at the top (status bar) and 34 px at the bottom (home indicator) on notched devices. Ignoring these areas leads to prototypes that look unrealistic during evaluation.

Items.Text: Frame presets for iOS, Android, and common web resolutions are available in the properties panel.
Safe areas represent system-reserved screen regions where interactive content should not be placed.
Using a device frame plugin or mockup overlay improves realism during peer presentations.
Designing at 1× and exporting at 2× or 3× maintains clarity on high-density displays.

Elements.Title: Organising Screens with Flows
Elements.BodyText: Grouping related frames into named flows helps both the design team and evaluators understand which screens belong to which user journey before prototype wiring begins.
Elements.Notes: Flows are a Figma prototype concept that sets the starting frame for a defined user path. Each flow can have its own starting point, making it easy to demo individual features separately.

Items.Text: A flow represents one complete user journey, such as onboarding, checkout, or settings.
Starting frames for each flow are marked in the prototype panel and become entry points during preview.
Naming frames sequentially, such as Login-01, Login-02, helps maintain spatial order on the canvas.
Colour-coded frame backgrounds can visually distinguish flows during design reviews.

Topics.Title: Building a Component Library
Topics.Summary: Guides students through converting repeated design elements into reusable Figma components, and using variants to manage multiple states of a single component efficiently.

Elements.Title: What Is a Component?
Elements.BodyText: A component is a reusable design element defined once as a master and instantiated across screens, so that changes to the master propagate automatically to all instances.
Elements.Notes: Explain the Main Component versus Instance distinction clearly. Students often edit instances not realising they can detach them, or accidentally edit the main component instead of an instance.

Items.Text: The main component is the single source of truth stored in the assets panel or a dedicated page.
Instances inherit all properties of the main component but can have overrides applied locally.
Editing the main component updates all instances across the file simultaneously.
Detaching an instance converts it to a regular frame, breaking the inheritance link.

Elements.Title: Creating Components from Existing Elements
Elements.BodyText: Any frame, group, or selection of elements can be converted into a component via the right-click menu or keyboard shortcut, after which it is accessible in the assets panel for reuse.
Elements.Notes: Best practice is to build components on a dedicated 'Component Library' page and then use them on design pages. This prevents accidental edits and keeps the library visible and searchable.

Items.Text: Select an element and press Ctrl/Cmd+Alt+K to create a component instantly.
Naming components with a slash notation such as Button/Primary groups them hierarchically in the assets panel.
Components should be self-contained with no dependencies on parent frame sizing.
Adding a thumbnail description in the component properties helps teammates identify correct usage.

Elements.Title: Component Variants
Elements.BodyText: Variants allow a single component to encapsulate multiple states — such as default, hover, disabled, and active — organised in a variant container that designers can switch between at the instance level.
Elements.Notes: The variant property grid works like a truth table: each combination of property values maps to one variant frame. Encourage students to map out all required states before building to avoid messy variant containers.

Items.Text: Variants are added within a single component set defined by one or more named properties.
Each variant property, such as State or Size, can hold multiple values separated by commas.
Switching variants on an instance preserves local text and icon overrides where layer names match.
Variant naming must be consistent across all states to enable smooth prototype interactions.

Elements.Title: Slots, Nesting, and Component Composition
Elements.BodyText: Complex UI elements are best built by nesting simpler components inside a parent component, a pattern called component composition, which maximises reuse and reduces maintenance overhead.
Elements.Notes: For example, a Card component might nest an Avatar component, a Tag component, and a Button component. Changes to any nested component automatically update all cards that use it.

Items.Text: Nested components are treated as instances inside the parent and retain independent override capability.
Component composition keeps individual components small, focused, and easier to test.
Avoid over-nesting, which can make the layers panel hard to navigate and slow design tool performance.
Published team libraries allow components to be shared and reused across multiple Figma files.

Elements.Title: Using the Assets Panel and Team Library
Elements.BodyText: The assets panel centralises access to all components, styles, and plugins, and team libraries extend this to share design tokens across an entire organisation or project team.
Elements.Notes: For student group projects, publishing a shared team library early in the project ensures all members use the same components. Walk through the publish flow in the File menu.

Items.Text: The assets panel search bar filters components by name, speeding up placement on canvas.
Colour and text styles can be published alongside components to enforce design tokens.
Team library updates require members to accept incoming changes to stay in sync.
Enabling a library in a file adds all its components to the local assets panel.

Topics.Title: Auto-Layout for Responsive Elements
Topics.Summary: Introduces Figma's auto-layout feature as the mechanism for creating frames that automatically resize and reflow their contents, enabling button, card, list, and navigation components that adapt to varying content.

Elements.Title: What Is Auto-Layout?
Elements.BodyText: Auto-layout converts a frame into a container that automatically arranges its children in a horizontal or vertical stack, adjusting size based on content, padding, and spacing rules.
Elements.Notes: A common first example is a button whose width expands as label text grows. This removes the need to manually adjust frame sizes whenever content changes — a major time saver in iterative design.

Items.Text: Auto-layout is applied via the design panel or Shift+A keyboard shortcut.
Direction can be set to horizontal, vertical, or — in newer Figma versions — wrap for grid-like layouts.
Padding and gap values control the internal spacing between the container edge and its children.
Auto-layout frames can be set to hug content, fill the parent, or have a fixed size.

Elements.Title: Sizing Modes: Hug, Fill, and Fixed
Elements.BodyText: Each dimension of an auto-layout frame or its children can independently use hug, fill, or fixed sizing, giving fine-grained control over how space is distributed within a layout.
Elements.Notes: Hug is ideal for buttons and tags. Fill is ideal for items in a list that should share available space equally. Fixed is used when a container must never resize, such as a sidebar of set width.

Items.Text: Hug content makes the frame shrink to the minimum size that contains all children.
Fill container makes a child expand to consume all available space in the auto-layout direction.
Fixed sizing locks the frame to an explicit pixel dimension regardless of content.
Mixing sizing modes within nested frames is the key to complex responsive layouts.

Elements.Title: Spacing, Padding, and Alignment
Elements.BodyText: Auto-layout exposes independent padding controls for top, right, bottom, and left, as well as gap settings and alignment options that determine how children are positioned within the container.
Elements.Notes: Auto space between option distributes children evenly across the container, similar to CSS justify-content: space-between. This is useful for navigation bars and toolbars.

Items.Text: Independent padding inputs replace the need for invisible spacer elements previously used as hacks.
Gap controls the uniform space between adjacent children in the stack direction.
Alignment options include start, center, end, and baseline for text-heavy containers.
The space-between distribution mode pushes the first and last children to opposite edges.

Elements.Title: Building Reusable List and Card Patterns
Elements.BodyText: List items and card components are the most common applications of auto-layout, and building them correctly enables entire list sections to reflow automatically when items are added or removed.
Elements.Notes: Demonstrate adding a new list item to an auto-layout list frame — the frame expands automatically. Then show the same behaviour inside a card. This visual demo typically resonates strongly with students.

Items.Text: A list frame set to vertical auto-layout with hug height expands downward as items are added.
Card components with auto-layout maintain consistent internal padding regardless of content length.
Wrapping auto-layout allows items to flow to a new row when horizontal space is exhausted.
Combining list auto-layout with component variants enables state-driven list items such as selected or unread.

Elements.Title: Auto-Layout and Component Interaction
Elements.BodyText: When auto-layout frames are used as or within components, size changes triggered by variant switching or text overrides propagate automatically, eliminating manual resizing during prototyping.
Elements.Notes: This is particularly powerful for form error states: switching a text input component to its error variant causes the error message label to appear and the surrounding form container to expand seamlessly.

Items.Text: Variant switches that reveal or hide nested elements cause parent auto-layout frames to resize automatically.
Text overrides on labels update container sizes without breaking padding or spacing rules.
Auto-layout combined with variants is the foundation of production-ready, data-driven prototypes.
Testing auto-layout behaviour with realistic content lengths prevents layout breakage during evaluation.

Topics.Title: Interactive Prototyping and Connections
Topics.Summary: Covers the Figma prototype panel, showing students how to wire frames and components with interactions, transitions, and overlays to create a navigable, realistic user flow for evaluation.

Elements.Title: The Prototype Panel Overview
Elements.BodyText: The prototype panel replaces the design panel when prototyping mode is active, exposing controls for adding interactions, choosing triggers, selecting actions, and configuring transitions between frames.
Elements.Notes: Switching between Design and Prototype tabs is a common source of confusion for new users. Emphasise that interactions are added in the Prototype tab, not the Design tab.

Items.Text: Prototype mode is activated by clicking the Prototype tab at the top of the right panel.
Hovering over a selected frame reveals a blue interaction handle used to drag connections to other frames.
The prototype panel displays all interactions attached to the currently selected element.
Device and background settings in the prototype panel control how the preview window is rendered.

Elements.Title: Triggers and Actions
Elements.BodyText: An interaction consists of a trigger — the user event that starts it — and an action — what happens as a result, such as navigating to a frame, opening an overlay, or scrolling to a position.
Elements.Notes: On click is the most common trigger for desktop flows. On tap is the equivalent for mobile. Encourage students to also explore On hover and While hovering to add realism to dropdown menus.

Items.Text: Common triggers include On click, On tap, On hover, On drag, and After delay.
Navigate to moves the prototype from the current frame to a specified destination frame.
Open overlay places a target frame on top of the current screen without replacing it.
Scroll to jumps the viewport to a specific position within a scrollable frame.

Elements.Title: Transitions and Animation
Elements.BodyText: Figma provides built-in transition types — Instant, Dissolve, Smart Animate, Move In, Move Out, Push, and Slide In — that control how the screen changes during navigation, adding polish to the prototype.
Elements.Notes: Smart Animate matches layers with identical names across two frames and tweens their properties, producing fluid motion that mimics native animations. It requires consistent layer naming — another argument for good naming hygiene.

Items.Text: Instant transition switches screens with no animation, suitable for simple click-through prototypes.
Dissolve fades between screens and is appropriate for modal or full-page transitions.
Smart Animate interpolates shared-named layers across frames to simulate micro-interactions.
Easing curves such as Ease In, Ease Out, and Spring control the feel of animated transitions.

Elements.Title: Scrollable Frames and Fixed Elements
Elements.BodyText: Figma frames can be configured to scroll vertically or horizontally, and individual elements can be pinned to remain fixed during scroll, enabling realistic navigation bars and sticky headers.
Elements.Notes: To create a scrollable frame: set the frame height to the viewport height, extend content beyond that height, enable vertical scrolling in the prototype panel, then set the content as overflow visible or clip. Fixed position is set per layer, not on the frame.

Items.Text: Scroll behaviour is enabled per frame in the prototype panel with Vertical or Horizontal scroll options.
The visible frame height defines the viewport; content extending beyond it becomes scrollable.
Layers can be fixed to the frame during scroll by enabling the Fix position option in the design panel.
Horizontal scrolling is commonly used for carousels, gallery rows, and tab bars.

Elements.Title: Overlays and Modal Patterns
Elements.BodyText: Overlays allow a second frame to appear on top of the current screen without navigating away, enabling modals, drawers, tooltips, and dropdown menus within a single prototype flow.
Elements.Notes: Overlay background dimming can be configured in the interaction settings. Setting Close when clicking outside is essential for realistic modal dismiss behaviour.

Items.Text: An overlay is triggered by connecting an element to a target frame using the Open overlay action.
Position presets include Centered, Top, Bottom, Left, Right, and manually specified offsets.
Background dimming adds a semi-transparent layer behind the overlay to focus user attention.
Overlays can themselves contain interactive elements, enabling multi-step modal flows.

Elements.Title: Previewing and Sharing the Prototype
Elements.BodyText: The Figma prototype preview launches a full-screen interactive session directly from the browser, and the share link exposes the same experience to peer evaluators without requiring a Figma account.
Elements.Notes: Prototype links differ from design file links. Share the prototype link specifically, not the editor link, to ensure evaluators see the interactive flow rather than the canvas. Test the link in an incognito window before submitting.

Items.Text: Press the Play button in the toolbar to open the prototype preview in a new browser tab.
The prototype share link can be set to allow anyone with the link to view.
The starting frame for the preview is defined by the flow start point set in the prototype panel.
Presentation mode hides Figma's UI and displays only the prototype within the selected device frame.

Topics.Title: High-Fidelity Design and Visual Polish
Topics.Summary: Focuses on the visual design properties — typography, colour styles, imagery, and iconography — that elevate a wireframe to a high-fidelity mockup representative of the intended final product.

Elements.Title: Defining and Applying Colour Styles
Elements.BodyText: Colour styles store named fill or stroke values that can be applied across the design and updated globally, functioning as the visual equivalent of CSS custom properties.
Elements.Notes: Encourage students to define a minimal palette of primary, secondary, neutral, and semantic colours before detailing any screen. This prevents colour drift across team members working in the same file.

Items.Text: Colour styles are created in the design panel by clicking the four-dot style icon next to a fill.
Naming styles with a token hierarchy such as Brand/Primary or Feedback/Error enforces consistency.
Updating a colour style propagates the new value to every element using that style instantly.
Colour styles support both solid fills and gradients, enabling rich background and overlay treatments.

Elements.Title: Typography Styles and Text Hierarchy
Elements.BodyText: Text styles standardise combinations of font family, size, weight, line height, and letter spacing, ensuring typographic consistency across all screens without manual reapplication.
Elements.Notes: A minimal type scale might include H1, H2, Body, Caption, and Label styles. Connecting these to a base font size makes scaling for accessibility straightforward later.

Items.Text: Text styles capture font, size, weight, line height, and letter spacing as a reusable definition.
Applying a text style decouples visual appearance from the text content, making global updates trivial.
Establishing a clear type hierarchy guides the user's eye through screen content in intended order.
Google Fonts and locally installed fonts are both supported in Figma for text style definitions.

Elements.Title: Working with Images and Fills
Elements.BodyText: Figma supports image fills on any shape or frame, enabling realistic photo placement for profile pictures, banners, and product imagery within the mockup.
Elements.Notes: Placeholder images from services like Unsplash can be inserted directly via the Figma Unsplash plugin, saving time during the design stage. Remind students that final images should match intended content closely for meaningful evaluation feedback.

Items.Text: Image fills are applied by selecting an element and choosing Image in the fill type dropdown.
Fill modes include Fill, Fit, Crop, and Tile to control how images scale within their container.
The Unsplash plugin and similar resources provide royalty-free placeholder imagery directly on canvas.
Cropping and positioning are adjusted with the Edit image button that appears in the toolbar.

Elements.Title: Icons and Vector Assets
Elements.BodyText: Icons reinforce meaning in UI design, and Figma supports SVG import, the built-in icon resources, and community icon libraries to provide scalable, stylable icon assets.
Elements.Notes: Icons imported as SVG become editable vector paths in Figma and can be recoloured using fill styles. Using a consistent icon set from a single library avoids the visual inconsistency of mixing styles.

Items.Text: SVG icons imported into Figma are fully editable as vector paths and scale without quality loss.
Community icon libraries such as Material Icons and Feather are available as Figma plugins.
Placing icons inside auto-layout frames ensures correct alignment and padding with adjacent text.
Applying a colour style to an icon fill allows global recolouring when brand colours change.

Elements.Title: Effects: Shadows, Blurs, and Overlays
Elements.BodyText: Figma's effects panel provides drop shadows, inner shadows, layer blurs, and background blurs that add depth and realism to interface elements such as cards, modals, and frosted-glass navigation bars.
Elements.Notes: Overuse of shadows is a common beginner mistake. Encourage students to use a single consistent shadow token for elevation levels rather than custom values on every element.

Items.Text: Drop shadow values include X offset, Y offset, blur radius, spread, and colour with opacity.
Multiple shadow layers can be stacked to simulate complex elevation or glow effects.
Background blur creates a frosted-glass effect on frames positioned over other content.
Effects should be captured as styles where possible to enforce consistency across the design.

Topics.Title: Building and Submitting the Group Project Prototype
Topics.Summary: Brings together all prior skills into a structured project delivery process, guiding student groups through collaborative construction, self-review, peer evaluation setup, and final submission of a shareable Figma prototype.

Elements.Title: Project Scope and Screen Inventory
Elements.BodyText: Before building, each group should define the exact set of screens required for their prototype, mapped to identified user tasks, to prevent scope creep and ensure complete coverage for evaluation.
Elements.Notes: A screen inventory is a simple table listing each screen name, the user task it supports, and its completion status. This document doubles as a progress tracker during the build phase.

Items.Text: A screen inventory lists every frame required and its relationship to a defined user task or flow.
Prioritise screens that represent the core user journey before adding secondary or edge-case screens.
Agree on a shared definition of done for each screen before work begins, including component usage and style compliance.
Review the inventory at regular team check-ins to surface blockers early.

Elements.Title: Dividing Work Across Team Members
Elements.BodyText: Effective team collaboration in Figma requires clear ownership of files, pages, or components, combined with a shared component library to ensure visual consistency regardless of who designs each screen.
Elements.Notes: A practical split is to assign one member to maintain the component library, one to each major user flow, and one to oversee prototype wiring and final QA. Roles can rotate across modules.

Items.Text: Assign ownership of specific pages or frames to individual team members to avoid edit conflicts.
All team members must use components from the shared library rather than creating ad-hoc elements.
Schedule a daily or session-based sync to merge work and resolve any visual inconsistencies.
Use Figma comments to flag questions or review requests without disrupting the file structure.

Elements.Title: Self-Review and Design QA
Elements.BodyText: Before sharing with peers, each group should conduct a structured self-review against a design quality checklist covering layout consistency, component usage, interaction completeness, and content accuracy.
Elements.Notes: Common issues found during self-review include missing back navigation connections, placeholder text left in final screens, misaligned elements not on grid, and inconsistent use of colour styles. A printed checklist helps teams be thorough.

Items.Text: Verify that all prototype connections are complete and that no frame is a dead end.
Check that colour and text styles are applied consistently and no ad-hoc values remain.
Confirm that all screens use components from the shared library rather than detached copies.
Review content for placeholder text and replace it with realistic, representative copy.

Elements.Title: Setting Up for Peer Evaluation
Elements.BodyText: Preparing the prototype for peer evaluation involves setting the correct starting frame, configuring share permissions, and providing a brief written description of the flows evaluators should test.
Elements.Notes: Provide evaluators with a one-paragraph description of the prototype context, the target user, and which flow to begin with. This reduces the cognitive overhead of orienting to an unfamiliar product during evaluation.

Items.Text: Set the prototype start frame to the most logical entry point, typically a home or login screen.
Share the prototype link with comment access so evaluators can annotate their observations.
Include a brief written context note either in the Figma file description or alongside the shared link.
Test the prototype link in an incognito browser session to confirm it works without editor access.

Elements.Title: Conducting and Receiving Peer Evaluation
Elements.BodyText: Peer evaluators interact with the shared prototype as a simulated end user, documenting usability observations, navigation breakdowns, and visual inconsistencies using Figma's comment tool.
Elements.Notes: Encourage evaluators to narrate their thought process as they navigate, noting where they feel confused or where they expected something different to happen. This qualitative data is often more actionable than ratings.

Items.Text: Use Figma comments pinned to specific frames to document precise observations rather than general notes.
Note any dead-end screens, unclear affordances, or visual elements that do not match expectations.
Evaluate both the interactive flow completeness and the visual design quality as separate dimensions.
Provide at least two constructive suggestions for improvement alongside any identified issues.

Elements.Title: Iterating Based on Feedback
Elements.BodyText: After receiving peer evaluation, groups prioritise and address identified issues within the remaining session time, applying fixes directly in Figma and updating the shared prototype link.
Elements.Notes: Teach students to distinguish between quick fixes — broken links, missing labels — and structural changes that require component or layout rework. Quick fixes should always be addressed first within constrained time.

Items.Text: Triage feedback into critical issues that block navigation and cosmetic improvements that enhance polish.
Resolve broken prototype connections before addressing visual refinements.
Document changes made in response to feedback to support reflection and academic submission.
Re-share the updated prototype link and notify evaluators that revisions are available.
